claims.text: Single-crystal FeNiCrMn has anomalously weak yield-strength dependence on strain rate in the elastic-to-plastic transition regime.
Yield onset in single-crystal FeNiCrMn is dominated by thermally activated kink-pair nucleation and migration of screw dislocations.
Dislocation nucleation at specific defects is not the dominant mechanism for yield onset in this alloy.
A deformation-induced phase transformation is not the dominant mechanism for yield onset in this alloy.
Atomic-size mismatch produces severe local lattice distortion in FeNiCrMn.
The initial FeNiCrMn single crystal has a metastable FCC structure.
The initial material is free of precipitates and secondary phases.
The proposed loading range is 10^-4 to 10^3 s^-1 and 77 to 600 K.
Crystal orientation should be selected to maximize screw-dislocation character.
Severe local lattice distortion impedes dislocation glide.
Severe local lattice distortion gives screw dislocations in FeNiCrMn high Peierls barriers.
At low temperature, kink-pair formation has a high activation-energy barrier and controls screw-dislocation motion.
Kink-pair-controlled yielding remains relatively insensitive to strain rate until a phonon-drag threshold is approached.
Yield strength will decrease strongly as temperature increases from 77 to 600 K.
Yield strength will have a low strain-rate sensitivity exponent over 77 to 600 K.
Stress-strain curves will show serrations caused by kink-pair dynamics.
Traditional FCC metals such as Cu and Ag are more strain-rate sensitive because they have lower Peierls barriers and are governed by phonon drag or defect nucleation.
Significant grain-boundary effects in a polycrystal would invalidate the proposed single-crystal yield mechanism.
Hydrostatic pressure will suppress a potential FCC-to-BCC or FCC-to-HCP transformation and thereby isolate dislocation mechanisms.
Observation of an FCC-to-BCC or FCC-to-HCP transformation as the primary mode at yield onset would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial FCC phase is called metastable, whereas the boundary states that the hypothesis applies where the FCC phase is stable. This may reflect kinetic retention versus thermodynamic stability, but that distinction is not stated.
